title: The seven-peg braid in the Sallow weaving archive
public_context: A fictional weaving archive keeps a conservation memo about planning cords across a set of pegs. The note concerns group-of-three layouts used in craft work. It is written for practitioners who plan an arrangement before selecting cord and tension for a completed piece.
source_title: Sallow Archive conservation memo on the seven-peg braid
source_text:
The Sallow Archive uses the name seven-peg braid for a planning pattern in which each working pair of pegs is joined once by a three-peg cord group. The memo treats the pegs as seven distinct points and each cord group as a set of three distinct points; the order in which a group is spoken does not create a second group. The pattern is useful on paper when a maker wants every pair to meet in one planned group before choosing cord thickness or tension.

The archive's named example uses Sedge, Kite, Lumen, Moss, Reed, Saffron, and Thistle. One cord joins Sedge, Kite, and Moss; another joins Kite, Lumen, and Reed; a third joins Lumen, Moss, and Saffron. The remaining groups are Moss with Reed and Thistle, Reed with Saffron and Sedge, Saffron with Thistle and Kite, and Thistle with Sedge and Lumen. Those seven triples are the complete pattern in the memo, not a sample from a longer hidden list.

Each triple contains three unordered pairs, so seven triples provide twenty-one pair incidences. Seven distinct pegs have twenty-one unordered pairs in total. A check of the listed groups finds no repeated pair: for example, Sedge meets Kite in the first group, Reed in the fifth, and Thistle in the seventh, while those three pairings do not recur elsewhere. The same check across the list shows that every pair occurs once. Each peg therefore appears in three groups, since its six pairings are covered two at a time.

The construction is compact, but the memo cautions that pair coverage is only a layout property. It does not say that every pair bears equal strain, or that a finished braid will survive repeated pulling. No load test is included, and no maker is named as the inventor of the arrangement. A conservator can use the pattern to compare where contacts are planned, then separately test the material and knotting method.

The note records that a trial layout was pinned on a board before a cord was cut, but it does not describe the board's dimensions or the cord's fiber. Nor does the archive say whether every workshop used the same named version. The seven triples and their pair counts are enough to check the combinatorial design. They do not establish when the pattern was first woven, how well it performs under load, or whether its name was used outside the archive's fictional workshop record.

evidence: The memo treats the pegs as seven distinct points and each cord group as a set of three distinct points

supported_claims.claim: The memo provides seven specific triples as the complete pattern.
evidence: Those seven triples are the complete pattern in the memo, not a sample from a longer hidden list.

supported_claims.claim: Seven triples of three points yield twenty-one pair incidences, matching the twenty-one unordered pairs among seven pegs.
evidence: Each triple contains three unordered pairs, so seven triples provide twenty-one pair incidences. Seven distinct pegs have twenty-one unordered pairs in total.

supported_claims.claim: The listed design contains no repeated pair, so every pair occurs exactly once.
evidence: A check of the listed groups finds no repeated pair: for example, Sedge meets Kite in the first group, Reed in the fifth, and Thistle in the seventh, while those three pairings do not recur elsewhere. The same check across the list shows that every pair occurs once.

evidence: Each peg therefore appears in three groups, since its six pairings are covered two at a time.

explicit_negatives.claim: The pair-coverage property does not assert equal strain for every pair.
evidence: It does not say that every pair bears equal strain

explicit_negatives.claim: The memo includes no load test.

licensed_inferences.claim: Any two distinct pegs in this pattern share exactly one cord group.
licensed_inferences.rationale: There are twenty-one possible pairs, the seven triples account for twenty-one pair incidences, and no pair repeats. Therefore each possible pair is covered once.

licensed_inferences.claim: The repeated degree of three at every peg follows from the design's one-time coverage of each peg's six pairings.
licensed_inferences.rationale: Each three-peg group contributes two partner pairings to each peg it contains. Covering six distinct partners exactly once therefore places each peg in three groups.

consistency_questions.question: How do the listed triples and pair counts justify the claim that every peg pair shares one group?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: The seven triples contribute twenty-one pair incidences, the seven pegs have twenty-one possible pairs, and inspection finds no repeated pair. Since the listed pattern is complete, all possible pairs occur exactly once.

consistency_questions.question: What follows about each peg's group count from pair coverage, and what physical property remains unestablished?
consistency_questions.reference_answer: A peg has six partners, and each triple containing it accounts for two of those partners; one-time pair coverage therefore places it in three groups. Equal strain and load durability remain unestablished because there is no load test.
